paragraphs.heading: A civilisation of the Bronze Age
paragraphs.text: The Indus Valley Civilisation was a Bronze Age society in the northwest of South Asia. It lasted from 3300 to 1300 BCE and was at its mature height between 2600 and 1900 BCE. It spread across much of today's Pakistan, northwestern India and northeast Afghanistan. It ranked, with Egypt, Mesopotamia and China, among the four centres of the ancient world, and it covered more ground than Egypt and Mesopotamia put together.

paragraphs.heading: Built along rivers
paragraphs.text: The civilisation grew up on the plain of the Indus River, and along a set of year-round rivers fed by monsoon rains that once ran near the Ghaggar-Hakra, now a seasonal river in northwest India and eastern Pakistan. It is named after the Indus, on whose plains its early sites were found and dug. Recent research suggests the Ghaggar-Hakra rivers turned seasonal around the time the civilisation shrank, roughly 4,000 years ago. In its mature phase its core ran 1,500 kilometres up the Indus and its tributaries. Around that lay a much bigger region, up to ten times as large, shaped by the Indus culture and economy.

paragraphs.heading: Planned cities
paragraphs.text: Its cities were known for careful town planning, houses of baked brick, elaborate drains and systems for supplying water. They also had clusters of large buildings that were not homes, along with skilled crafts and metalworking. Mohenjo-daro and Harappa probably grew to hold between 30,000 and 60,000 people. At its peak the whole civilisation may have numbered between one and five million.

paragraphs.heading: From farms to towns
paragraphs.text: Farming appeared around 6500 BCE in Balochistan, at the edge of the Indus plain. Over the following thousands of years, settled life spread into the plains and set the stage for villages and towns to grow. This more organised way of living raised the birth rate. The death rate rose as well, because people living close to their animals caught more contagious diseases.

paragraphs.heading: Drying out
paragraphs.text: In the 3rd millennium BCE the land slowly grew drier, and this may first have spurred people to build cities. In time the same drying cut the water supply enough to bring the civilisation to an end and scatter its people to the east. The language its people spoke is not recorded directly, and its family is uncertain, since the Indus script has never been deciphered. Some scholars favour a link with the Dravidian or Elamo-Dravidian language family.

paragraphs.heading: Finding the ruins again
paragraphs.text: The first modern accounts of the ruins came from Charles Masson, who had deserted from the army of the East India Company and who travelled through Punjab in 1829. His major find there was Harappa, a large city in the valley of the Ravi, a tributary of the Indus. He made many notes and drawings, but wrongly thought the place had been described during Alexander the Great's campaigns. Later, Alexander Burnes stopped there too, noticing the old baked bricks and how local people were carrying them off. Harappa is the civilisation's type site, the site that archaeology by custom uses to name it. It was the first of the civilisation's sites to be dug up, early in the 20th century, and it gives the civilisation its other name, Harappan.
